newsitem.title: USA: Fed policy said focused on growth/inflation tie.
newsitem.headline: Fed policy said focused on growth/inflation tie.

text.p: By tightening credit in a low inflation environment, the Federal Reserve has proven that U.S. monetary policy is firmly anchored on the notion that rapid growth fuels higher prices, Fed watchers said on Tuesday.
"There is considerable underlying strength in the U.S. economy," noted Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Nesbitt Burns Securities.
"They are sufficiently concerned to take the opportunity to slow the economy right now to prevent inflationary pressure," Cooper added.
Citing "persisting strength in demand" and "risk of inflationary imbalances," the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.

The rate hike was the first since February 1, 1995 -- the final move in a rapid-fire tightening cycle that inaugurated an era of preemptive policy for a central bank often blamed for running behind the inflation curve.
"The Fed will raise rates again in May to reduce growth sufficiently to get more slack in labor markets," predicted Cooper, one of the few Fed watchers who, early this year, forecast a March hike.
Upcoming FOMC meetings are scheduled for May 20 and July 1-2.

The six-month Eurodollars is trading at 5.75 percent, indicating the market has priced in a second move in the benchmark overnight interbank lending rate no later than the August 19 or September 30 meetings.
Cooper, calling the Fed's move a "preventive measure," said "the economy does not have to slow that dramatically to prevent inflation."
The FOMC, in its announcement, also described the tightening move as a "prudent step."
Fed sources told Reuters the Fed looks at the Gross Domestic product on a six-quarter average.
By the end of 1996, the six-quarter GDP average was rising by 2.8 percent, a sharp acceleration from an average of 2.0 percent a year earlier and 2.3 percent six months earlier.
The rising trend coincided with a decline in the unemploymnent rate below 5.50 percent and an uptick in the wages component of labor costs.
But Cooper said the Fed does not necessarily have a huge task ahead since "It's not the growth of the past but the growth of the future that matters to the Fed."
Cooper expected the Fed to remain in a tightening mode until growth "is brought down to 2.5 percent."
But Ken Bercuson, chief economist at SBC Warburg, expected the Fed to have to follow a very restrictive path that would involve "about 150-basis-point hike in the year ahead."
Bercuson made the point that, in order to quell inflationary pressures in a buoyant economy, the Fed would have to "bring growth down to 1.0 percent and keep it there."
Bercuson argued that a year of GDP growth at around 1.0 percent was needed to offset the 3.2-percent growth recorded in 1996 and restore a non-inflationary 2.0-percent trend.
The SBC Warburg chief economist also pointed out that "the U.S. economy no longer is very rate-sensitive" due to the wide array of financing sources now available to businesses and households.
The Fed did not raise the 5.0-percent discount rate and commercial banks did not immediately follow the funds rate hike with a prime rate increase.
"They have to raise rates a lot since this is not a particularly rate-sensitive economy. Consumption has been accelerating," Bercuson stressed. "The consumer is propelling this economy forward."
But David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International, said the Fed will need to reevaluate consumer spending and its policy outlook at midyear.

"There is some ambiguity about the nature of the acceleration we have seen in recent months. By early May, we'll have greater insight in what underlies consumer spending," said Resler, who expected the Fed to need more inflationary evidence to justify its ensuing moves.

"With the GDP price deflator at its lowest in 30 years, you don't have a strong case for aggressive tightening since the Fed's responsibility is to prevent inflation from going up -- not to prevent the economy from growing," Resler said.
"With inflation still low and no sign that it is rising, it would not be possible for the Fed to tighten very much without incurring the wrath of Congress," Resler concluded.
Bercuson and Resler were among only seven analysts who forecast the March tightening as early as February.
